en: Composed by the Tiantai śramaṇa Zhìràn of the Tang Dynasty:
An Explanation of the "Chapter on the Merit of Rejoicing.
Regarding the title of this chapter, there are four layers of names that also correspond to the four *siddhāntas* (purposes), though they do not follow a sequential order.

In principle, one must provide an exegesis that ensures the meanings correspond; however, since the subsequent chapters all pertain to the two gates of the manifested and the real (honji-suijaku), although both meanings are explained here within the context of "counteractive treatment" (pratipakṣa), the meaning also extends to the other three types of "perfection" (siddhi). This is because the text of the "Chapter on Rejoicing" (Anumodanā-parivarta) already compares [the merit] following the extinction [of the Buddha], while the beginning of the "Five Grades" (Pañca-varga) corresponds in meaning to the head of the "Fourfold Faith" (Catur-śraddhā) in the present age. Since both derive their rank from hearing the "Chapter on Increasing Longevity" (Āyuṣ-pravardhana-parivarta), it is necessary to describe both the present and the past gates together.

The following section, the "Chapter on the Merits of the Dharma Master," corresponds precisely to the stage of the four faiths in the present life and the stage subsequent to sympathetic joy; therefore, two interpretations are not maintained here, as they have already been fully explained within the "Chapter on Differentiation" and the "Chapter on Sympathetic Joy."

Furthermore, this is a praise of the efficacy of the five kinds of Dharma-preachers, who are able to enter the stage of the fourfold faith through the six sense organs as if they were present. Since the section beginning with "Never-Disparaging" (Noble Never-Disparaging) refers collectively to the *Lotus Sūtra*, how could it pertain solely to the provisional traces?
If that is so, then since the preceding passages also mention the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, they too should possess both [aspects].
Answer: Because the latter has not yet been taught.
In the first section concerning the world, the names are first explained briefly, followed by a detailed explanation, and finally a summary.
Since the initial [brief] explanation governs what follows, the names are explained first; within that first text, "conformity" (*anuloma*) comes first, followed by "joy" (*pramuditā*).

The initial explanation regarding the phenomena and principle within "conformity" (suí) is simply a distinction between the provisional and the real; since understanding this provisional and real means they are neither provisional nor real, they are non-dual and without distinction—this is precisely the phenomenon and principle of conforming to [the provisional] to open it up and reveal the real.

Next, in the detailed explanation of the joy of "releasing," the term "one's own person" refers to the power of both phenomena and principle within the traces [of the Buddha’s teaching]. Because principle possesses phenomena, it can bring joy to others; because phenomena possess principle, one can rejoice for oneself.
Furthermore, because it is non-dual yet dual, one rejoices in both self and others; because it is dual yet non-dual, one realizes that there is neither self nor other.
Next, in the second explanation following the section "Hearing the Profound," the text first explains how [the teaching] accords with the complete array of provisional and ultimate merits.
Next, from "Rejoicing that one possesses wisdom" onwards, there is another explanation of rejoicing in the merit of possessing both compassion and wisdom.

Although it is said that rejoicing for oneself is truly for the sake of benefiting others, and although it is said that rejoicing for others is truly for the sake of manifesting oneself, it is therefore stated that one must possess both wisdom and compassion; because one has heard the sutra oneself and is further able to teach others, it is only when compassion and wisdom are fully complete that it is called "rejoicing."
Moreover, since at the very beginning of hearing the sutra, practice and vows arise simultaneously, each phrase and each verse benefits both oneself and others.
Now, although this beginner’s stage establishes the path of self-cultivation as primary, one likewise uses the power of vows to rejoice in the welfare of others.
The phrase "expedient means and reality" (*upāya-tattva*) below concludes the two preceding meanings to establish the title of this chapter.

"Expedient means and reality" concludes "conformity," while "knowledge and abandonment" (*jñāna-prahāṇa*) concludes "joy. Compassion and mercy constitute the transformation of others; since transforming others belongs to liberation, and liberation belongs to abandonment, these are further categorized as belonging to the world, because one rejoices in the matters and principles concerning both oneself and others.

Regarding the section "Furthermore, in accordance with principle" within the counteractive measures (*pratipakṣa*), concerning the primary gate (*mūla-mukha*): first there is the explanation, followed by the summary of the chapter.
Within the initial explanation, first comes "conformity" (*anuloma*), followed by "joy" (*prāmodya*).

Regarding the section on "Following," there are three parts: first, the formal explanation; second, from "That is extensive" onwards, the conclusion establishing the mutual integration of the characteristics of contemplation regarding phenomena and principle;
and third, the final summary.
In the initial passage, principle is presented first, followed by phenomena.

Regarding "the principle first": if one’s faith is directed toward the long-term, that faith must necessarily rely upon the principle. This principle is no different from the subtle principle within the traces; it merely indicates that the focus lies in the distant origin and that merit is attributed to actual realization. Because the principle is profound and the time is remote, it is called "profound and far-reaching."
Regarding the term "faithful compliance": since one has long heard the principles, how could one dare to harbor secret doubts?
Therefore, there is not even a hair’s breadth of doubt concerning these long-standing principles.

Next, regarding "compliance with phenomena," this refers solely to the Tathāgata’s manifestations for the benefit of sentient beings from his original attainment. Within the provisional traces (*jì*), there is only a horizontal discussion of the modes of transformation; however, within the fundamental reality (*běn*), one must add the vertical aspect of long duration. Thus, the long duration of transformation is termed "vertical" and the vastness of transformation is termed "horizontal," because at every stage in between, [the Buddha] pervades the ten directions.
"Universal pervasion" (*gaigen*) refers simply to the horizontal and vertical omnipresence. Regarding the contemplation of their characteristics:

there is no principle that can be manifested without transformation, and there is no transformation that does not manifest principle. Thus, by observing the immediate traces of phenomenal activity, one perceives the remote fundamental principle. Furthermore, although the fundamental and the phenomenal differ, they are inconceivably one; yet, while they are one, the fundamental and the phenomenal remain distinct. Therefore, it is said: "non-dual, yet dual."
Question:
What is the difference between the distinct [nature] and the two [natures]? Answer:

There are two [aspects], which generally encompass both the fundamental (hon) and the manifested (jaku), and specifically correspond to multiple objects, because within both the fundamental and the manifested there are each different characteristics.

Next, from "Although there are two" onwards, it is again subsumed and integrated: whether fundamental or manifested, all are revealed through the three thousand [realms] as wondrous events that accord with principle.

Third, regarding the conclusion beginning with "In this way": this merely summarizes the preceding points that the non-duality of phenomena and principle, while appearing as two, are equally designated as the single "One Accordance.

Regarding the section beginning with "The Tathāgata," it explains the joy [of hearing]. First, by means of time and person, it refutes the provisional traces; thus, for over forty years and throughout the seven stages of expedient means, it was not until the present sutra that these were not yet fully realized. Without the realization of expedient means, there would have been no way to manifest the fundamental reality. Looking back at those times when one had not heard it, one rejoices in having now obtained the opportunity to hear it.
Next, from "Rejoicing for Myself" (*qing wo*) onwards, there is the formal explanation of joy.

Third, from "With the mind of an ordinary person" (*yi fanfu xin*) onwards, the characteristics of the joyful mind are clarified: through hearing one knows; based on knowing, vision arises. Only a Buddha knows the Buddha’s long-lasting lifespan, and only a Buddha sees the Buddha’s long-standing realization of the true principle. Hearing about the Buddha is no different from being the Buddha himself; thus, one enters the stage of contemplative practice (*guanxing wei*).
The phrase "In this way" below concludes the characteristics of the contemplation; it also carries the meaning of the non-duality of the horizontal and vertical dimensions.
The principle of the ultimate *dharmadhātu* encompasses both the horizontal and vertical, and thus one should speak of it as "profound and vast," though here the expression is abbreviated.

Regarding the phrase "vast and boundless" and so forth, this universally praises both the horizontal and vertical [dimensions of the Buddha's qualities]; because there is nothing with which to compare them and no equal to them, it is further described as "unequaled by equals."
One should also conclude by stating, "This is called joy"; its absence from the text is due to abbreviation.
From the words "The Buddha now" onwards, the title of the chapter is concluded: it is called "Counteractive" (*pratipakṣa*) because it removes doubts regarding phenomena and principle.
Regarding the section "The fiftieth person" and below, which explains the person, there are four parts:

first, the reiteration of the characteristics of the person, which is the reiteration of the stage; second, from "At first, there was only... and below, the reiteration of the following (anumodana); third, from "There was only... and below, the reiteration of the joy (muditā); fourth, from "Whoever hears... and below, the double reiteration of both following and rejoicing, followed by an exposition of the intent and a comparative calculation; and fifth, from "Who, having heard... and below, the conclusion and exhortation.
Within the section on comparative evaluation, there are again three parts:

first, it clarifies that one's practice is meager; second, within the stage of "conformity," there is only the principle but not yet the application of skillful means; third, within the stage of "joy," there is only benefit for oneself but not yet the ability to benefit others.
Next, from "the merit obtained" onwards, both types of rejoicing are explained as having great merit.

Third, from "the Tathāgata" onwards, the sūtra is directly cited for comparison; since it cites the figure of four hundred million *koṭis* from the subsequent passage, this is termed a "skillful analogy."

The analogy refers to the fiftieth person; therefore, it asks "how much more so for the first," because this is the first stage. Since this is the beginning of the fifth stage, how could one say "how much more so for the fifth stage"?
This is the commencement of the perfect position (yuanwei), hence it says "how much more so for the subsequent mind."
“Subsequent mind” refers to the ultimate stage.
Within the fourfold exhortation, there are two parts:
first, the exhortation by citing the purport of the sutra.
The term "Tathāgata" concludes the exhortation of the sutra and establishes the title of this chapter.
It causes one to advance toward principle and enter the stages; being able to give rise to the goodness of the Way is what constitutes a person.
"Jing" (景) means great, and it also implies admiration.

Regarding the phrase "as mentioned above," within the context of the first principle (*paramārtha*), "above" refers to the sections from the "Dharma Master" chapter through the "Upholding" chapter, as well as the four types of faith and five levels of practice within the "Discrimination of Merit" chapter.

Regarding the phrase "the assembly at that time," the following is intended to prevent those who might misunderstand: fearing that they would fail to perceive the greatness of the merit of the initial resolve (*prathama-citta*), and thus attribute all merit to higher stages while disparaging this initial resolve, he now demonstrates that although their practice was shallow, the merit was profound, thereby revealing the power of the Sūtra.
The phrase "Suddenly hears" introduces the *hamsa* and *kalaviṅka* as metaphors for the initial mind.

Because the holy words personally praise it, one is led to attribute the merit [to the Buddha] and have doubts removed; thus, the term "releasing and clarifying" (*shìrán*) is introduced to correspond to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
The section on "Haojian" (Good and Firm) and "Kalaviṅka" is fully recorded in the first and seventh notes of the *Zhi Guan*.
The passage beginning with "Rare indeed" concludes the establishment of this chapter.

The section beginning with "Non-Buddhists" employs comparative analysis according to the teachings; it first rebukes the various partial and limited views of non-Buddhists and others. Although the Small Vehicle may reach its own ultimate limit, it still cannot compare to even the very first stage of the Perfect Teaching’s position of sympathetic joy (*anumodana*).

When others refer to "the gate being crude" within the context of the Middle Way, it is because they have heard the name of the Middle Way prior to the stages (bhūmi), but have not yet directly contemplated it.

As for the passage beginning with "The Buddha now raises 'A'," this precisely clarifies that in the stage of the Perfect Teaching, the beginning and the end are non-dual; therefore, this is something absent from all other teachings.
Question:
The first letter A resides in the first dwelling; how does it realize the first category? Answer:

The names are distinct while the meanings are universal; however, if these are applied to the forty-two stages, they cannot be universally applied to the first stage. If applied to the six identities, even "principle-identity" (li-ji) is already applicable, let alone the first grade.
Now, since we clarify non-duality by means of perfect practice, it is applied universally here.
Within the question and answer, first the visible is questioned.
In the response, the phrase "this dharma" refers to the fact that the Dharma has been heard through successive transmission.
Regarding the phrase "that person," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"If there are śrāvakas who are able to resolve their minds [upon enlightenment], I likewise rejoice in them.
One should further inquire: since that refers to both [the bodhisattva and the śrāvaka] while this refers only to the latter, how can they be the same?
Answer: It is not because they are combined, nor because they are uncommon or distinct; rather, it is because we fear that their names might be confused when discussing their distinctions.

Furthermore, while those [terms] are words used for induction, these [terms] judge the actual merit of the initial mind. Therefore, in the former case there is no principle of generating the resolve (*cittotpāda*), whereas here it clarifies that one has already become established in accordance with the principle. Thus, although the names are the same, their realities are eternally distinct.

Regarding the statement, "The preceding chapter compared four types of persons": at the end of the "Chapter on the Distinction of Merit" (*Punyaparyāya-parivarta*), after the scriptural passages concerning the latter four types of persons had each been individually compared, there remained no comparison for the text of the first chapter; therefore, this present chapter was composed.

Therefore, the commentary at the end of the preceding chapter states: "Now, having fully listed the five chapters to compare them with the [first] four, the subsequent 'Chapter on Rejoicing' will compare the first chapter.

Regarding the phrase "seizing the opportunity": because the Buddha knew the capacity of the assembly and withheld it without speaking, Maitreya was moved to strike upon the Buddha's mind to inquire extensively about the initial text; only then did they realize that the merit of the latter four chapters is vast, and since the benefit to the assembly was even greater, it is called "seizing the opportunity."
"Southern" refers to south of the Yangtze River. Regarding the terms "superior," "inferior," and "equal":

the intention is that each subsequent stage being progressively superior is called "superior"; each subsequent stage being similar [to the preceding] is called "equal"; and each subsequent stage being progressively weaker is called "inferior. Thus, by means of the progressive inferiority, one illustrates the equal and the superior; if the merit of even the fiftieth person among those of inferior rank is still great, how much more so for those who are equal or superior, reaching up to the fiftieth?
Although the phrasing has not yet refuted the principle, it is not entirely incorrect; however, this merely uses what is progressively inferior to illustrate the initial stage.

Why then employ "equal" and "superior"? "Equal" implies that the beginning and end are similar, while "superior" implies that the latter excels the former; neither constitutes the proper limit for comparative evaluation.

As for the correct interpretation here: because past masters have criticized the explanation of the fifty stages as being contrary to the text and failing in principle, I shall now assist them by provisionally relying upon the gates of the teachings to establish the number of persons.

As for the fact that the *śikṣamāṇās* are not listed among the group of six classes of followers, this is merely a temporary omission made for the sake of matching the numerical count; how could it be that a *śikṣamāṇā* would not hear the sūtras?

Furthermore, there is no necessity to follow the perspective of the "gate of existence" (*bhava-mukha*) by treating the great bhikṣus as the primary members of the assembly. Although the number of people and gates here accumulates up to forty-eight, the intent is to clarify that each teaching and each individual, following a specific gate and practice, may all hear from the assembly of those at the Dharma-gathering.

Regarding the two interpretations: first, based on the meaning of the three teachings, those who were among the fifty people in the provisional teachings of the past have now heard the Perfect teaching;
second, those who have now again become fifty are all those who, upon hearing the sutra, have been revealed and fully realized as the four types of persons.

Therefore, it is impossible to enumerate them exhaustively; for now, we shall rely on the method of calculation and conclude with one set of seven, such as the seven generations and so forth—since the larger number is taken from among the seven, the total becomes forty-nine.
Regarding the phrase "all are teacher and disciple" and so forth, this is because they teach one another in succession.
As for the statement that "the very last person has no one to teach," this is said merely by way of a comparative assessment within a single period of time.

Regarding the phrase "the great seven" (*dai-shichi*) and so forth: the numerical system of this region was established by the Yellow Emperor and possesses two different conventions. In the lower system, one hundred thousand is called a *ok* (億);

in the upper system, one billion is called an *ok*. The same applies to the number seven; thus, multiplying seven by seven constitutes the "great seven," which, in the smaller [lower] system, amounts to forty-nine.
Together with the final person, this makes fifty; this is merely a provisional summation of their number.
The correct principle is as previously established in the refutation of the ancient masters; the passage beginning with "It is not so" below constitutes that point.

Regarding the "four modes of birth" (*catasro yonayaḥ*) mentioned in the *Sūtra*, some have extensively expounded upon their meaning in treatises based on the *Abhidharmakośa*, the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, and various other sūtras and śāstras. These are not essential for the present text; it suffices to have a general understanding of the six destinies (*ṣadgati*), as briefly indicated in the first fascicle [of this work] and the first commentary on the *Mohe Zhiguan*.
The four modes of birth are those from the womb, from eggs, from moisture, and by transformation.
Furthermore, in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Xian shi lun), another set of four modes of birth is established: first, birth through contact, which occurs due to sexual union.
Second, those born from smelling: when a male with lustful intent smells the organ-opening of a female, she immediately becomes pregnant.
Third, those born from sand: for example, when a female sparrow, with lustful intent, scatters sand, she thereby becomes pregnant.

The fourth is birth from sound (*śabda-ja*): for example, when a female peacock hears the cry of a male due to desire, she immediately becomes pregnant. These four types of birth encompass only those born from a womb (*jarāyu-ja*) and those born from an egg (*aṇḍa-ja*);

for those born from moisture (*sveda-ja*) and by transformation (*upapāduka*), it is sufficient that they are defiled by the scent of their place of birth, and such characteristics as these are not required.

Regarding the phrase "bestowing worldly happiness and uprooting the suffering of the fruit": it is called "worldly happiness" because one provisionally bestows the four requisites and the seven treasures;

it is called "uprooting the fruit" because it brings peace to the body of the fruit [of rebirth]; and it is called "uprooting the suffering of birth and death" because it enables one to attain the state of an Arhat.

Regarding the phrase "this is Brahma-merit": although this person instructs others so that they may attain the fruits of sainthood (*ārya-phala*), he himself has not yet attained such fruits; thus it is merely called "Brahma-merit," whereas only upon attaining the fruits of sainthood would it truly be called "saintly."
The phrase "now expanding upon this" refers to the text of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.

Among the various forms of merit, none is greater than that of Brahmā; therefore, in the *Śāstra*’s explanation of the marks adorned by a hundred merits, it treats the merit of Brahmā as a single unit of merit.
Based on such a calculation, the attainment of the four fruits of the śrāvaka path through this present sutra is likewise the merit of Brahmā.

Within this, there is yet another comparative calculation to determine the merit of hearing this sutra: by using the initial merit of all the sages as a standard to compare it with the final benefit of hearing the sutra, one sees that even the first thought of rejoicing in hearing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* surpasses the merit of those later sages, let alone the merit of the first sage himself.
Thus we know that worldly people, while looking at a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*), strive to seek crystal; having already encountered sunlight, they plot to use lamps and candles.

Regarding the terms "Sattva" and "Mahāsattva," these refer to three bodhisattvas viewed in relation to one another; for the time being, speaking in terms of relative magnitude, even a bodhisattva at the ultimate stage of skillful means (*upāya*) cannot yet equal the fiftieth person, let alone merely teaching others to attain the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*).
Regarding the term "noble merit" (*āryapuṇya*), it is so called because it belongs to the category of merit superior to that [of worldly merit].
However, in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, when comparing [merit] at the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*), the matter remains relatively easy;

now, to compare the noble merit at the initial stage of rejoicing (*anumodana*) is something that, were it not for the solemn intent of a Great Sage, how could one possibly believe in such a marvelous thing?

Therefore, we know that based on their practice alone, it is said: "This person practices the collateral [path], while the other practices the direct [path]. Consequently, this entire section cannot be described as collateral; it is entirely the direct track of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Regarding the merits herein corresponding to fifty persons, Zhiyi (Zhang’an) merely indicates the number without pointing to the specific scriptural passages.
Now, I shall briefly correlate them, combining every two merits into a single phrase:
first, a single location and sharp faculties.
Wisdom is not mute; the mouth is fragrant and the tongue is free from ailment.
When the mouth is free from ailment, it is without defilement.
It is neither black nor yellow;
it is neither sparse nor deficient;
nor is it uneven or crooked.
The lips do not hang down nor are they drawn up;
they are neither shrunken nor coarse and rough;
they are free from sores and likewise free from cracks.
Neither deficient nor impaired;
neither crooked nor thick;
neither oversized nor discolored.
It is not black and nothing about it is loathsome;
it is neither flat nor crooked or distorted;
it is neither black nor narrow.
Neither too long nor too short,
neither crooked nor anything but pleasing;
with beautiful lips and a beautiful tongue.
Fine teeth and excellent dentition;
a long, high, and straight nose;
a full face and high-arched eyebrows.
With long eyebrows and a broad forehead,
possessing the marks of a person of perfect symmetry;
having seen the Buddha and heard the Dharma.

Regarding the phrase "the preceding is the stage of similar merit" (*sabhāga-guṇa*) and so forth, this refers to what is stated in the "Chapter on the Distinction of Merit" (*Guṇavibhāga-parivarta*) concerning the "five grades after extinction. Since the Master sometimes follows the *Samantabhadra-buddhānusmṛti-sūtra* in judging that the five grades of practice (*pañca-vipākya-pada*) are situated within the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*), he refers to them as "similar."

If one points to the "Four Faiths" (*catur-adhimukti*), they correspond precisely to the "Similar Stage" (*sabhāga-avasthā*); furthermore, the "Chapter on the Initial Calculation of Merit" (*Prathama-puṇya-pariṇāma*) herein is the fifty-eighth. Since the first Dharma assembly is what was heard, it may be considered the first chapter; thus, the fifty-eighth must pertain to the very beginning of the stage of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*).
However, the title of this chapter, "Rejoicing" (*anumodana*), is not restricted solely to the beginning; it applies universally to all fifty individuals. Regarding the phrase "The practice...

followed by "and so forth," the specific characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the practice should be explained in detail: these fifty virtues may be fully possessed by a single person, or each may be possessed by one individual respectively; depending on their respective capacities, it is not necessary that they be possessed in their entirety.

In this verse, the five points from the preceding section on sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) are versified, whereas the question-and-answer portion is not, as it may be understood by analogy. Furthermore, the sequence within the section on hearing the sutra is slightly disordered; however, it can be understood by comparing it to its original order.

Regarding the "Chapter on the Merits of the Dharma Master": first, the title of the chapter is explained; next, the increase and decrease of merits are explained, which refers specifically to the merits of the Dharma master.

In the initial explanation of the title of the chapter, the four *siddhāntas* (purposes) are likewise applied; therefore, the conclusion below states: "Equipped with these four intentions. In the first passage, it concerns the *loka* (world);

next, from "the practitioner" onwards, it concerns the *puruṣakāra* (benefit for the person); next, from "clearly discerning" onwards, it concerns the *pratipakṣa* (remedy); and next, from "semblance-understanding" onwards, it concerns the *paramārtha* (ultimate meaning).

At the beginning of this section, the preceding chapter is first cited to explain the title in common with it; thus, the two characters "Dharma-master" (fǎshī) refer entirely to the preceding chapter, as it was also by means of five kinds [of persons] that they were designated as Dharma-masters. Therefore, it says, "as above."
Question:
Since this chapter states that these are the fruits of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*), why does the name of the Dharma Master refer back to what preceded? Answer:

The disciple penetrates both the beginning and the end, while the Dharma Master [penetrates] only two or three; as for the meaning, it also encompasses the latter two, or perhaps has not yet fully entered the stages. Why is this?
If one considers the five stages as entering within the six faculties, the five masters serve merely as the causes for the six faculties.

Even though the five grades are situated outside the six faculties (*ṣaḍāyatana*), the Five Teachers do not say that they cultivate meditative practice (*vipaśyanā-bhāvanā*); they merely claim that these grades are "penetrating" by virtue of recitation and exposition. Furthermore, this "penetration" extends at least to the second and third grades, and their exposition even encompasses the fourth and fifth; thus, for the time being, it appears to be generally applicable.

If one were to examine this by way of the specific stages, it refers exclusively to those who have not yet entered the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). Since that category is explained extensively under the name "Dharma Master," one must refer back to that [explanation] to clarify the meaning of the present term.

Since the title "Dharma Master" applies universally without distinction between those of the four levels of faith and the five grades of practice, the text points to that passage to establish the heading of this chapter.
As for "merit," the following section provides a detailed differentiation.
The initial reference points to the beginning of the first chapter, specifically indicating the fiftieth person.

Now, it is said that "above the five grades" refers to these six sense organs; because their merit is identical yet their status is eternally distinct, it is termed "the merit of the Dharma Master. Thus, it is called "the merit of the Dharma Master."

Regarding the phrase "adorned internally and externally" and so forth, it is explained in two stages: first, it is directly applied to the six sense faculties; second, from the words "Furthermore, from... onwards, it further advances by relying on the stage of reality (*bhūtatathatā*), meaning that from this stage of semblance (*sādṛśya*) up to the time of the first dwelling (*prathamabhūmi*), the universal manifestation of the form-body (*rūpakāya*)—and indeed at every successive stage up to the ultimate position—is fundamentally based upon these initial practices.

Regarding the phrase "the five faculties are likewise": when entering the stage of true reality (*bhūmi*), all six faculties possess both internal and external adornments. One perceives and hears the ten realms as an external transformation; the remaining three [faculties] are to be understood by analogy, and the same applies to form and the other objects.

Furthermore, if one speaks in terms of the "universally manifesting form-body" (*sāmbhogika-kāya*) as being "similar," then it may be understood as referring to the stage of semblance (*sādṛśa-bhūmi*).

Next, regarding the phrase "reciting and chanting" and below, which cites other masters: these five Dharma-preachers all give rise to a semblance-understanding (*sādṛśa-adhimukti*). For now, one must set aside the true stage (*bhūta-bhūmi*) of the universally manifesting form-body and instead take the stage of semblance as the present merit. Because the five masters and their five grades differ in terms of the true and the semblance, they are termed "worldly" (*laukika*).
Question:
Why does copying [the scriptures] purify the six sense faculties? Answer:
They share the same basis of right understanding.

Regarding the phrase "the four grades are likewise," this clarifies that the arousal [of the roots] is indeterminate; from the initial stage of sympathetic joy (anumodanā) up to the final stage of right practice, all involve the arousal of the six faculties. Why, then, must one necessarily pass through the five stages before entering the stage of semblance (sādṛśya)?

Regarding the term "furthermore" (*jia ran*): when comparing the initial stage to the subsequent ones, the initial stage is already able to enter; the latter four stages further add to what preceded them. As for the phrase "if similarity is thus," etc.:
within the stage of partial realization (*fen zhen*), the roots and purity are twice as great as before; because one is comparing the true (*zhen*) to the semblance (*si*), it is called "twofold."

Next, as for the person [of the second stage], they should diligently contemplate and cultivate the four kinds of samādhi, causing them to swiftly enter the subsequent faith; because each instance of faith looks back toward the preceding one, it is called "doubling" (bei).

Next, regarding the antidotes: one who possesses profound understanding and has heard extensively, as previously calculated, is termed "Great Power" (Mahāsthāmaprāpta), for only then can they eliminate doubts concerning the provisional traces.

Regarding the phrase "the very first of those with semblance-understanding" (*sādṛśya-bodha*) within the context of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), according to the *Samantabhadra-darśana-sūtra*, one who rejoices (*anumodanā*) is at the head of those with semblance-understanding; furthermore, the fiftieth person is at the beginning of that act of rejoicing, hence it is called "the very first."

Regarding the phrase "surpassing the ultimate limit of the two vehicles": the Arhat has already reached the ultimate; yet there is an ultimate that is even more ultimate. Even one who is free from doubt cannot equal the person who first rejoices by even a hundred-thousand-millionth part, as was calculated previously.

Regarding the phrase "beginning with the fingers" and so forth: by taking the initial stage of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) as the starting point, one reveals that it culminates in wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). If even the resolve of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) is ultimately non-dual from wondrous enlightenment, how much more so is this the case for those at the stage of the five ranks (*pañca-varga*) in relation to the six faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*)?

Regarding the "Virtues of the Six Faculties," the following is a direct explanation of the increase and decrease of these virtues. First, two schools are briefly presented; next, they are collectively refuted.
First, in the Guangzhai [school], there is no specific refutation in the text, yet their established positions are not appropriate.
Why is this? Each of the five types of Dharma masters attains the six sense faculties; how then could five masters together constitute six thousand? Therefore, each master possesses four hundred.
If there were three grades, even if they totaled one thousand two hundred, how could that constitute the six thousand merits of a single master?
How much more so for those of the three grades of capacity?
Therefore, the conclusion below refutes the notion that "the faculties do not rely on the text," let alone the claim that the ten wholesome actions are merely mundane (scattered) virtues.
As for the strength or weakness of the three faculties in this land, citing the text from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* is entirely inappropriate here.

In this text, the eyes, nose, and body have eight hundred [faculties], while the ears, tongue, and mind have one thousand two hundred; because the three—eyes, ears, and mind—are more powerful in their functions according to the *Śāstra*, they do not correspond [in number].

Furthermore, there are masters who take the *Guangzhai* (Light-Residing) number as three grades; yet in the present sutra, there are only eight hundred, one thousand, and two [thousand], so how can they further establish one thousand?
If the six sense organs were divided into three, it would mean that two halves would correspond to a whole, which is logically untenable.

The phrase "the various masters" below provides a general refutation; they have not yet understood the increase and decrease of the six sense organs as well as their merits and so forth in this present sutra.
Regarding the phrase "inconsistent with various teachings," this refers to the three sutras and one treatise listed below, other than the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

Why is this? Because the six sense organs confront the three thousandfold world of dust, yet beyond these dusts, they perceive and hear the four types of noble ones. Thus one knows that the power of the sutra assists the understanding of internal contemplation, giving rise to the semblance and partial realization [of the truth], universally permeating all the faculties; therefore, there are such functions as seeing and hearing.

Furthermore, some cite the six objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) within the realm as explained in the *Abhidharmakośa* and other texts to interpret the six objects mentioned here; however, this captures only a partial meaning and does not reflect the literal intent of the text, and is therefore not adopted.

Furthermore, among the six sense organs, the three—ear, nose, and tongue—do not require contact [with their objects]. The ear relies on non-contact for what is visible to it; the nose relies on non-contact for what is audible to it; and the nose relies on non-contact for the presence of odors. As for the two organs of the tongue and body, they must reach their objects: the tongue relies on reaching its object to manifest flavor, thus taking "transformation" as its function, while the body relies on reaching its object to manifest tactile images, thus taking "manifestation" as its use. Both, however, take the ten realms as their measure; they do not concern the small vehicle’s model of sense bases and objects confronting one another. Therefore, there is no need to speak of twenty-two types of form or eight kinds of sound.

If it were not so, the three thousandfold world-system would fundamentally not be something seen or heard by the fleshly eyes and ears of ordinary beings; why, then, do you say that they see and hear the three thousandfold world-system?
Furthermore, to further explain this as being deluded by the six sense objects due to the causes of devas, humans, and so forth, is even more contrary to the present intent.
In the section "The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Dàpǐn) departs," he directly cites three sūtras and one śāstra to refute the two preceding masters.
Next, from "Now, this sūtra" (*jīnjīng*) onwards is the formal exposition, which begins with the citation of sūtras and śāstras in two parts:
first, the actual citations; second, a brief conclusion.

Now, this sutra is fully equipped to refute [the opposing view]. Specifically, in the initial citation from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, it clarifies the prajñā of the six sense faculties. Is this not precisely because the "Examination of Merits" chapter compares and measures correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*) with the purity of objects and wisdom, showing they are without distinction or gradation? This passage does not yet mention their numerical count, but speaks only of their equality and purity.

The passage beginning with "If the six faculties... refutes the previous teacher; first it refutes him, and then the section beginning with "If one... employs a counter-interrogation (*pratyavamarśa*).
The phrase "and so forth" (*yathā-yathā*) indicates that more [arguments] should be added in parallel.
Citing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it likewise first cites the "roots" and so forth; the section beginning with "without distinction" is refuted in the same manner as before.
Next, citing the meaning of the *Śāstra* text regarding "the clarity of the power of the sūtra," it states that the power of the sūtra should not cause the roots to be superior or inferior.
Regarding the phrase "although not yet," etc.: although they have not yet entered the stages (*bhūmi*), their merit is equal to that of those who have entered them.
Next, he cites the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* to clarify the characteristics of mutual functioning; since they are already equal and mutually interpenetrating, how could the principle be partial?
The formal explanation is divided into four parts:

first, clarifying that the preceding four sections are contained within a single sutra; second, the actual interpretation; third, from "If one discusses... onwards, distinguishing between additions and omissions; and fourth, from "Similarity... onwards, determining the stages.
Next, there are two further sections:

first, regarding the methods for propagating the sutra, it clarifies that there are one thousand [instances] of equality; second, regarding the principle and the object, there are one thousand two hundred [instances].
In the initial desire to provide the correct explanation, the author further refutes the Guangzhai school.

Now, based on the "Peaceful Practices" chapter, we clarify the three karmas; this precisely accords with the "Dharma Master" chapter’s method for propagating the sutra, whereby one attains the purification of the six sense faculties.
The Guangzhai [commentary] simply states that the ten wholesome acts and the five kinds of Dharma-preachers together constitute the total number;

however, the present work clarifies that only when the count is complete does it state that the five kinds of Dharma-preachers each possess six thousand [qualities]. Therefore, we first take the three karmas and ten wholesome acts from the "Peaceful Practices" chapter as our basis, followed by the ten suchnesses of a single realm. When these are matched with the aspect of transforming others and the three items beginning with clothing, the sixty are fulfilled to constitute the perfect practice. Herein, the three karmas are themselves the six faculties; thus, they are not further paired with the six faculties, for once the merit of the three karmas is perfected, the six faculties are purified.

The section beginning with "The five kinds" clarifies that each of the masters purified the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya*). Next, the section beginning with "Furthermore, with one mind" correlates the objective realm (*ālambana*) with the practice (*caryā*); this is also an explanation based on the stage of mutual functioning and similarity, which is why it says, "A single organ universally possesses the six objects.
If explained from the perspective of the cause, however, it refers merely to the fact that within the contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-caryā*), the principle inherently possesses the six objects.
The section beginning with "If one discusses" clarifies the characteristics of increase and decrease, first explaining those very increases and decreases.

"Pure" refers back to the preceding *prajñā*. Regarding "among the adornments there are those that are full or deficient, etc.," this refers back to the preceding main scripture (*sūtra*); it lacks a reference to the treatise (*śāstra*), which merely equates the powers of ordinary beings with the clarity of the sages, and the physical eyes with the divine eye, and so forth.

"If one says 'twelve thousand,'" the following section distinguishes between the expansion and contraction [of time], which pertains to the present sutra; it discusses expansion and contraction based solely on what was previously equated.

"If one says 'pure,'" this reiterates the preceding *Prajñāpāramitā*; "'the six sense organs function interchangeably'" reiterates the preceding *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*; and "'also inconceivable'" reiterates the preceding citation from the śāstra.
The phrase "If [the practice is] partial" below concludes the refutation.

Regarding the phrase "Similar," in the section on determining the stages, it mentions "four wheels"; while the *Ratnakaranda-śrāvakabhūmi-sūtra* (瓔珞經) enumerates six wheels in full, we shall employ four for now.

If one relies on the fifty-two stages, only the *Śrīgarbha-sūtra* (瓔珞經) provides a complete and systematic presentation; therefore, we shall borrow from it to establish the meaning of the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*). The only difference lies in whether the stages are considered "severed" or "unsevered"; the Iron Wheel-turning King remains in the position prior to the four wheels, which corresponds to the Ten Faiths (*shixin*).

The phrase "the third mind" is likely an error; it should read "the second. Because faith (*śraddhā*) is general while diligence (*vīrya*) is specific, the latter is used here as an illustration. Regarding the detailed delineation of the stages from beginning to end, this is roughly as found in the *Bodhisattva-śīla-vyākhyā* (Pusa jie shu) and the section on the "Subtlety of Stages" in the *Xuanwen* (Xuanyi). Furthermore, the specific characteristics of cultivation and entry into the stages are fully detailed within the "Stages of Practice" (*Chuxing*) section of the *Mohe zhiguan*. Since the present text only clarifies the merits of the Dharma Master, these matters have been omitted.

The following scriptural text consists of six chapters on the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*). Following the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, each faculty possesses ten aspects; these are identical in meaning to those presented here, differing only in their degree of authenticity.
Thus, both the "five" and the "ten" equally encompass both the true and the semblance [knowledges].
Furthermore, the "five" and the "ten" differ only in being a division or a synthesis.
However, the Hīnayāna does not regard the nose and tongue as supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and regarding the mind, it fails to provide a clear explanation for its separation from the other three.

The various Mahāyāna sūtras also possess the six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā), yet they do not speak of the six faculties (ṣaḍindriya); this is merely because they treat them as secondary and minor matters while simultaneously rejecting the Lesser Vehicle.

Now, the present sūtra and the *Avataṃsaka* are definitive teachings (nītārtha). Moreover, since their cultivation and manifestation differ from those of the Lesser Vehicle, and their respective bases are distinct, they are already different from the latter; how much more so in comparison to others?

In the initial discussion of the eye-faculty, the cultivation and manifestation of the true divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) and so forth were not yet addressed; rather, it was stated that the physical eye alone can see the great trichiliocosm, hence the phrase "born of one's parents."
If one discusses its function, it already surpasses the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).

The impure divine eye can see what is below but not what is above; though the vision of a Brahmā King may pervade the great trichiliocosm, upon reaching its limit, it is obstructed by the wind-circle (*vāyu-maṇḍala*).
Those with the purity of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya-viśuddha*) are not like this.

Therefore, it should now be stated that there are "similar Buddha-eyes," and so on up to "similar five eyes. Consequently, it should also be stated that they see the two vehicles as well as Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and others; for by analogy with the ears and nose, these must necessarily be present.
Regarding the statement, "Seeing the interior and exterior of the great trichiliocosm constitutes the divine eye," this refers, for the time being, to the scope of seeing coarse and subtle forms.
Regarding the statement, "Seeing karmic causes and conditions constitutes the dharma-eye," this is because such things are not seen by the power of the divine eye.
Regarding "seeing karma and seeing purity": karma has distinctions while purity has none; seeing these two objects simultaneously expresses the Middle Wisdom (madhyama-jñāna).
Furthermore, because it can perfectly subdue [the afflictions], it is the Buddha-eye (buddha-cakṣus).

Regarding the phrase "The Great Sūtra says," etc., this is a specific citation showing that the physical eye can perform the function of the Buddha-eye, thereby serving as proof for the passage beginning with "born of one's parents."

The passage beginning with "Because of the Buddha-eye" reiterates the previous four sections refuting the Guangzhai school, as well as the present thesis and the summary of the "expansion and contraction" passages, thereby establishing the correct interpretation.

"Purity of the eye faculty" refers back to the preceding *Prajñā*; "possessing the five" refers back to the preceding text of the *Śāstra*; and "adornment" refers back to the preceding *Sūtra* and so forth. One should also say that they mutually possess the five faculties to refer back to the *Nirvāṇa*, though it is omitted in the text for brevity.

The five faculties that follow below are each exactly like this; however, from here until the end of this section, they are abbreviated together, merely marked with "and so forth" (*yún yún*), or only one or two sūtras are cited. This is done so that when they are further quoted below, the reader will not lose the overall sense.

Furthermore, each of the five lower faculties is explained in two ways: first with respect to their capacity to see, hear, and so forth, and second with respect to the objects seen, heard, and so forth; thus they are mentioned twice.
The faculty of hearing can be seen.

Because the sense faculty of the nose is most thoroughly examined, the mutual functions regarding the nasal faculty are further explained; by analogy, the other faculties should also be understood in this way, though the text is merely abbreviated.

If, according to the intent of the response regarding the tongue-faculty, one must first know the dharma-realm of flavors before causing those flavors to transform into something delicious, how much more so when all six faculties are pure—how could the tongue-faculty alone be inferior?

Regarding the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*), it is said that "non-delusion" is the provisional (*prajñapti*), "non-attachment" is emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and "simultaneous illumination" is the middle way (*madhyamā*).

Regarding the mind-faculty (*manendriya*), it is said that "the first month, the fourth month," and so forth, are explained as the signified (*lakṣya*), because they all penetrate the preceding five [faculties] as being non-dual.

If one explains it in terms of objective phenomena (*vastu*), there is only the sixth faculty; therefore, there is no need for an exhaustive discussion regarding the objects corresponding to the six faculties.

However, while the "Chapter on Rejoicing" compares [the merit] with that of the first chapter, and the "Chapter on Distinguishing Merit" directly clarifies the four levels of faith and the five stages of practice, the current "Chapter on the Merits of the Dharma-Preacher" merely clarifies the merits of the six sense organs in their semblance stage. The "Chapter on Never-Despising" clarifies the purification of the six sense organs as the present-life and future-life retribution for one who propagates the sutra; the "Chapter on Supernatural Powers and Entrustment" clarifies the power and function of propagating the sutra by means of the fruition-stage practitioner to encourage its circulation; and the "Chapter on the King of Joy," "Chapter on Wonderful Sound," and "Chapter on Avalokiteśvara" clarify the functional capacity of those who have partially realized the Truth to propagate the sutra. Thus, it should be known that the determination of the stages is self-evident based solely on this sutra; other methods of determination based on the *Śāstra* represent but one approach, as can be seen below.

Therefore, from the "Chapter on Rejoicing" (*Anumodanā-parivarta*) onwards, there is no need for an exhaustive explanation of the characteristics and appearances of objects; it is sufficient to briefly indicate the textual structure to manifest its transmission and propagation, whereby the merit of its circulation will naturally be understood.

Commentary on the Chapter on the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging: Since this chapter first cites the past, one should know that the "Never-Disparaging" [section] already contains five chapters that can serve as proof for the cause, and the subsequent attainment of the six faculties serves as proof for the fruit; therefore, it is called "Citing Evidence."
Jiaxiang fully explains the texts of the preceding chapters of the present sutra by dividing them into seven distinct sections:

first, he correlates the two preceding chapters with the three chapters on merit in the present text—namely, the *Anumodanā* chapter as the lower section, the *Dharmabhāṇaka* chapter as the middle section, and the present chapter as the upper section.

Second, in contrast to the two preceding chapters which describe merit across the three periods of time, this chapter on "Rejoicing" concerns the present, while the chapter on the "Dharma Master" concerns the future; thus, this chapter surpasses them.
Third, in contrast to the "Merit of the Dharma Master," which clarifies the fruit, this chapter elucidates the cause.
Fourth, it clarifies that sentient beings have only the One Vehicle.
Fifth, whereas the preceding section clarified the Buddha’s prediction, this section clarifies the bodhisattva.
Sixth, whereas the preceding section clarified the exhortation to merit, this section clarifies the eradication of transgressions.
Seventh, citing scriptural evidence to prove that the six sense faculties [are purified].

Regarding the "three grades," the *Anumodanā* (Rejoicing) chapter permits the lower grade, whereas the *Dharmabhāṇaka* (Dharma-preacher) chapter and this present passage both purify the six faculties; how then could there be a distinction between middle and superior?
How much more so for one who first slanders this [teaching] and falls into hell.

Regarding the "three periods of time": the chapter on "Rejoicing" refers to the period after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa; the chapter on the "Dharma Master" shows that five kinds of merit are accomplished in the present life; and although the chapter on "Never-Disparaging" involves the past, it clarifies what occurs in subsequent lives.
Regarding what is called cause and effect, both purify the six sense faculties; how could they be divided into two distinct categories?
Regarding what is called the One Vehicle, it pervades all sections of the canon; how could it be limited to this alone?
It is indeed appropriate that the Buddha and Bodhisattvas grant predictions (vyākaraṇa) specifically regarding the section on "Distinguishing Merits.

As for the mention of "sin and merit," it means that one incurs sin by slandering [this teaching] now, while a believer gains merit; yet, since slander was produced in the preceding passage, how could there not be sin?
In the section on "Rejoicing," one is born together with bodhisattvas who possess *dhāraṇīs*; how could such keen faculties and wisdom be merely a matter of merit?

As for the statement regarding the extinction of offenses: those who give rise to slander fall into hell, which constitutes the creation of offenses; yet, when their faculties are purified at the moment of death, how could this be merely the extinction of offenses?
[The Dharma Master: "In the midst of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), the subtle aggregates (*skandhas*) manifest and evolve; what transgression would not be extinguished?

As for the statement that cites a specific event to prove the purification of the six sense organs (*ṣaḍindriya-viśuddhi*), why does it not say that by propagating even a single phrase one will necessarily purify the six organs? This is because the original text cited in the chapter speaks of 'inconceivable' [attainment]."
Examples such as these could not be cited in full; therefore, they are briefly described here to stimulate insight.
Consequently, I shall now further explain this by means of six points.

Among these, the first point is considered in relation to the preceding chapter of the present sutra, while the remaining five all consider the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* in relation to what preceded it.

First, previously we fully propagated the literal text of the sutra; now, we shall briefly propagate its underlying meaning. Therefore, rather than engaging in recitation, we shall simply proclaim the name of "Not Disparaging.

Second, while the minor scriptures may inspire faith, they do not yet serve as the two causes [for the purification of the six faculties]; whereas this present sutra, even when slandered, can induce the purity of the six sense organs.

Third, while other sutras clarify only the transformation through conformity and the propagation of the teaching, this chapter clarifies the transformation through contrariety and the penetration of principle.
Fourth, while the provisional and the real indicated by other sutras still remain separated, what is revealed in this chapter is none other than the fourfold unity.
Fifth, while the traces manifested in various sutras are not yet exhaustive, this chapter simultaneously manifests both the fundamental and the trace aspects.
Sixth, whereas other sutras state that those with overweening pride will eternally fall into suffering, this chapter enables them to believe, submit, and follow accordingly.

Although Jiaxiang’s *Seven Meanings* does not fail to offer some insights, it has not yet reached a profound realization; only by grasping the underlying intent herein can one follow its various examples.
Question: Is it not a grave error to record that those who saw [the Buddha] all said, "You shall all become Buddhas"?
Or is it that those who propagate [the teachings] in this final age have lost their way? The *Dharmapada-śāstra* states:
"This bodhisattva knows that sentient beings possess buddha-nature, and thus does not dare to treat them with contempt."
Regarding the fact that both treatises were composed by Vasubandhu yet differ in their presentation of *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena), how could they be contradictory?

They merely expound the sūtras so that each may attain its own pedagogical intent. If a single person were to compose [only one] treatise, then all explanations would necessarily be identical; however, it is impossible to exhaustively apply the Abhidharma (*Dharmapada*) of the Hīnayāna to explain the Mahāyāna. Thus, we know that those treatises were composed to expound the Vaipulya (Mahāyāna) teachings themselves. This is why Kāśyapa lamented over his "ruined seed," until at the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, that ruined seed was restored to life; Vasubandhu then used his treatises to expound upon this very point.

If one discards the Tathāgata’s texts that reveal the ultimate truth while remaining mired in the Bodhisattva’s teachings that propagate provisional means, the transgression of biased attachment is unsurpassed, and the error of such a mistaken application is evident.
Now, at the beginning of this chapter on "Text," the fourfold unity is fully present; it is explained by means of these four. Within this, there is first an enumeration and then an explanation.

Regarding the mention of the *Dharmapada-śāstra* (*Fahua lun*) in the explanation: since that *Śāstra* permits that this bodhisattva knows all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, he goes to pay homage to anyone he sees. How could it be that among these four assemblies there are none who have extinguished their lineage, yet he would falsely speak of them?
If it does exist, then the fault lies with Vasubandhu for not stating it in his treatise; if the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* is correct, then the fault lies with Aśvaghoṣa and with the Buddha.

Yet, rather than first holding him accountable for the fault of failing to revere [the teachings], you still consider him a person who propagates the sutras; how could there be such errors as mispronouncing or misrecording them, which would cause one’s six sense organs to be purified in this life and the next?

Regarding the phrase "The true cause pervades universally," etc.: because the nature-virtues (xingde) pervade both delusion and enlightenment, as well as cause and effect, the conditions and the understanding (yuanliao) are said to be seeds inherently present. Thus, the two causes are explained by way of these nature-virtues, in contrast to the newly perfumed (xin xun) factors which constitute the attained virtues of cultivation (xiude). These three serve as the causes that transform into the fruit.
The Bodhi and Nirvana within the fruit are termed the "nature of the fruit," which is the nature of the fruit-of-fruits.

If one distinguishes cultivation from nature, it refers simply to the attainment of the conditions (pratyaya) and the understanding (pariniṣpatti) through cultivation; upon reaching the fruit, these are called Bodhi and Nirvana. Understanding is simply wisdom (jñāna), and wisdom is named Bodhi; conditions are simply severance (prahāṇa), and severance is named Nirvana.
Furthermore, when the three causes of nature reach the stage of fruition, they are designated as the three kinds of bodhi; what was termed "conditions" is now termed the three kinds of nirvana.

If one says that sentient beings possess both cause and effect natures, then the five Buddha-natures are all present within sentient beings, pervading all places. However, while abiding in the state of cause, the nature of the fruit is called "cause"; when in the state of fruition, one encompasses the cause and it is called "fruit. Although the names differ, their underlying dharma remains eternally as it is.

Regarding the phrase "the former is the causal teaching" (*hetu-pratyaya*) and so forth: the first five passages, beginning with "internally harboring the understanding of non-contempt," refer to this.
As for "the latter is the Perfect Teaching," this is a classification according to the teachings (*yōkyō*).
This follows from the "Samādhi of Seeing Reality.

In contrast to the partial [teachings], there are four; in contrast to the provisional, there are five, because in other teachings there is never the statement that sentient beings are themselves Buddhas.

Since the preceding causes and conditions should fully comprise the four *siddhāntas*, within the fivefold textual structure, the first two sections correspond to the first two *siddhāntas* (the worldly and the individual), while the latter three correspond to the remaining three. This is as detailed in the Preface, where the four "ones" are likewise correlated with the four *siddhāntas*.
The phrase "and so forth" indicates that while the three teachings were previously contrasted, here we concern ourselves solely with the Perfect Teaching.

Regarding the statement, "In the past, through my sympathetic joy, I obtained [benefits] in this life and in future lives," this serves to clarify the purpose of the coming discussion; thus, the subsequent text says, "As I was about to pass away, I heard in full the Buddha King of Majestic Sound preaching the Lotus Sūtra, whereby I attained the purity of the six faculties and further increased my lifespan"—this refers to retribution in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma-vedanīya*).
"After the end of his life, he again encounters two thousand *koṭis* of Buddhas, all equally named Candrasūryapradīpa," refers to the retribution in this very life (*sadyaḥphala*).

"By these causes and conditions, he again encounters two thousand *koṭis* of Buddhas, all equally named Meghasvararāja, and again encounters ten million *koṭis* of Buddhas," refers to the subsequent retribution (*āyatyām phalam*).
Within this present retribution, one attains the purification of the six sense faculties; therefore, the merit of propagating this sutra is no small matter.

The intention in speaking of these three benefits lies in its circulation. Since the three types of retribution for the former "Never-Disparaging" Bodhisattva were so manifest, how could we not circulate it today?

Some say: "This is intended to manifest that the majestic power of the 'Practice of Peaceful Dwelling' (anle-xing) is peerless; thus, I shall perform the Practice of Peaceful Dwelling as the 'Not-Disparaging' (bu-qing) practice.

Now, it is said that one who practices the 'Practice of Peaceful Dwelling' is at the initial stage of propagating the sutra; therefore, its ritual form differs from that of the 'Not-Disparaging' in ten respects.
Why is this? That one sits peacefully upon the Dharma-seat and speaks according to the questions asked; this one, however, goes to pay homage because he sees the fourfold assembly from afar.
That one provides answers only when there is something difficult to ask; this one, however, proclaims [the teaching] forcefully even while being struck and pelted with tiles and stones as he walks.
That person constantly delights in sitting in meditation in secluded places, whereas this one does not focus on recitation but seeks to proclaim himself among the assembly.
That person deeply loves the Dharma and does not speak much; this one, despite being slandered with falsehoods, still insists on praising himself.
In that [text], the initial question asks how to read and expound this sutra; here, it merely speaks of the single phrase "circulating [the teaching] to become a Buddha.

In that [text], one initially cultivates contemplative observation (li- guan) to observe the eighteen kinds of emptiness; here, one merely harbors the understanding of the single phrase "becoming a Buddha."
That refers to the transformation Buddha personally teaching to elucidate the body of space; this refers to the body of space teaching to elucidate the matters of transformation.
That refers to the distant indication within a dream that one shall attain the great fruit; this refers to the oral proclamation of the teaching on attaining the causes for Buddhahood.

The former [text] uses the parable of loosening the topknot to reveal the provisional nature of the Two Vehicles; this [text], however, uses the binding of conditions to manifest the reality of the One Vehicle.
The former preserves formal protocols because it accords with the transformative teachings; this, however, discards constant traces because it employs counteractive transformation.
The former enumerates the methods of superior practice to win over people, while the latter specifically cites past individuals to facilitate the understanding of the supreme Dharma.

Regarding the phrase "the basis of the matter and the basis of the matter": it refers generally to the Buddha King of Majestic Sound (Vaiśvānara) of the past as the basis for the matter of Never-Disparaging (Adīnapramada); thus, it is called the "basis of the matter."
Within this, because it specifically concerns the events from the time of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna (Vaiśvānara) during the age of Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja, it is called the "Past Deeds" (*pūrvayoga*).

Regarding the phrase "attaining the grand tenet of the correct teaching," etc., two lines are first presented; the section beginning with "named 'Constant'" explains these two lines. First, the initial line is explained, followed by the section beginning with "the profound respect of the Unconquerable One" (*Adhimātra-gaurava*), which explains the second line.
"Great" (*kō*) signifies vastness;
"principle" (*shū*) signifies sublimity.

Regarding the two aspects of origin and trace, the fourfold and singlefold teachings, and the three natures, the primary exposition of the Great Principle does not exceed the true aspect (*shinjitsu-sō*). This true aspect is precisely the eternally abiding Buddha-nature (*busshō*); this refers to the "principle" as the ultimate goal, rather than the "principle" as the essential substance.

Although it is said that throughout the various teachings of this one lifetime—whether they are combined, supplementary, or purely Hinayana; whether they are mixed auxiliary gates, concealed, or sublated—the texts are broad and the matters extensive, such that each teaching differs and each flavor has its distinct meaning. Yet, [the Lotus Sūtra] does not merely proclaim twenty-four characters; it possesses both headings and explanations, fully describing cause and effect. Since the causes are the three natures and the fruits are the three virtues, how much more so when the fourfold "oneness" simultaneously benefits oneself and others? It directly points to the two causes as the Dharma proclaimed by the Bodhisattva Never Disparaging; therefore, it is called the "Grand Doctrine."
The school that reveals reality does not transcend the fourfold unity; since each of these four unities is itself but three, we shall now interpret the text based on this fourfold unity.

Within this, first we explain the grand tenet of the fourfold unity; second, we cite the text to determine the stages; third, from "Rejoicing" onwards, we clarify the meaning of rejoicing; and fourth, from "Respecting the person" onwards, we conclude the meaning of rejoicing.
The first section of the text has two parts:
first, the迹门 (Ji-men) reveals the ultimate reality; second, the本门 (Ben-men) opens up the near [to reveal the far].
The former clarifies the merit of rejoicing in the Dharma Master, demonstrating the benefit for those who hear the exposition of the sutra after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
This citation ensures that both the propagator and the listener of the past attain great merit.

Whether propagating or listening, both are simultaneously connected to the "original" and the "traced" (honji-suijaku); how could it be merely a matter of becoming a Buddha? Therefore, one must explain this by means of both gates; only then does it accord with what was proclaimed by Namo-fujō (Namu-afukō), coincide with what was expounded by Oon (Ongon), harmonize with the principle of the five grades, and allow those of the six sense organs to find their ultimate refuge. The phrase "fully hearing" completely expresses the original and the traced, for is it not the case that the title *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* does not pertain to a single gate alone?

Regarding the passage in the "Manifestation" (biaoji) section that states, "The one named Constantly Not-Light (Niangchangbuling)," and so forth, one should carefully employ the textual characteristics to interpret the four "ones," ensuring they accord with the intent of this current text.

Although those of overweening pride have established names for this, it is already the result of the bodhisattva’s practice and vows; thus, it causes the one who inscribes the record to mysteriously accord with its reality.

As for the phrase "From 'even unto' to 'seeing afar,' which represents the fundamental four-in-one," this simply uses the distant to represent the distant, and so on, until we reach the four-in-one of the original ground inherent in the [Lotus Sutra] chapter on "Never Disparaging."
Therefore, because they were not yet capable of manifesting the fundamental [truth], it was instead represented by means of dwelling at a distance.

Even within the traces (*traces*), the manifestation of reality is still forcefully constrained by the four aspects of the traces; how much more so could the fundamental reality be accepted immediately?
The traces are manifest while the source is esoteric; thus, one knows that "the four and the one" constitute the grand tenet of this sutra.

Next, regarding the citation of evidence for the determination of stages, the phrase "not exclusively" and so forth indicates that because [the practitioner] does not engage in recitation or chanting, they take "not disparaging others" as their exclusive practice, stating "only performing prostrations. This is because the method for entering the stage is not limited solely to the five kinds of Dharma-preachers; whether self or other, whether through faith or the Dharma, whether obscure or manifest, whether extensive or concise—therefore, even proclaiming a single phrase brings about a merit of no small measure.
Therefore, the current text judges this to belong to the stage of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*), serving as the direct cause for the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*). Some say:
it is not exclusively "mixed."
Now it is said that this merely clarifies non-intermixture; it does not specifically correspond to the specific.
Someone asks: For what reason is there ritual and custom?
I shall now answer this.

The methods for a bodhisattva’s transformation of conditions have no single fixed standard; because their sole concern is benefiting others, they establish these rituals. Seeing that the principle of the sentient beings' nature is equal to the principle of the fruit, the source of paying homage to sentient beings and paying homage to the Buddha is not different—this is the practice of self-cultivation.
It is intended to cause sentient beings to give rise to the aspiration for the fruit; what is this aspiration for the fruit?
We merely pay homage because we respect that principle; how much more so should one revere and honor it when one has realized the principle of the fruit!
Furthermore, it says:

"You all practice the bodhisattva path and shall attain Buddhahood. Is this not striking me so as to cause me to cultivate the perfect cause? This refers to those who comply in the present; they are those of faith-practice (śraddhā-carita) and also those of dharma-practice (dharma-carita).

Now, benefits may be either hidden or manifest; the manifest is near while the hidden is distant. Though the distant is like a superior intention that one does not receive in the present, its sound is taken into the heart; by the fault of slandering and reviling, one falls into the evil realms, yet through the power of hearing what is compliant and submissive, one encounters the Tathāgata Never-Despising (Anatamanā), leading to the present day where one is again enabled to enter this assembly. For this reason, even arrogance can still become a remote cause; how much more so for hearing and believing—how could these lack immediate benefit?
Therefore, those who slander become the cause for the "poisonous drum"; this may be understood through both detailed and abbreviated expositions.
By adorning oneself and attributing the merit of transformation to oneself, one purifies the six sense faculties through the mutual cultivation and refinement of self and others.

Some cite here from the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* the passage on paying homage to those who know the Dharma, as well as the passage from the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* concerning bhikṣus paying homage to laypeople;
however, this interpretation is incorrect.
In the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the constant ritual manifests the intent to revere the Dharma; because he requested instruction from him, [the Buddha] set aside formal etiquette and condescended.

In the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, having already received profound grace upon hearing the Dharma, Vimalakīrti set aside considerations of transgression to offer his respect, thereby not adhering to fixed rules.

If the correct principle of the Mahāyāna is a transcendent and eternal norm, it likewise does not require one to perform worldly salutations; nor is it lightly established that all practices must differ from this, nor is it intended to proclaim a teaching that fails to harmonize the Great and Small Vehicles.
Some say that if a Bodhisattva does not perform this prostration, they commit an offense.
Now, I maintain that for an offense to exist, it must be based on established regulations; since there is no such text in the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*, there is no prohibition for minor matters.
Furthermore, it is said:
"A bodhisattva must necessarily guard against natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*), but may exceed the prohibitory transgressions (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*).
Now I ask: if one necessarily exceeds the prohibitory transgressions, can such an excess be called "maintaining" [the precepts]?
If one transgresses, they cannot be called "upholding" [the precepts]; if they break them, they are not Bodhisattvas.

However, when forgetting a transgression to save sentient beings, what is most valued is the well-being of those beings. If the beings are at peace, why distinguish between the prohibitive and the essential nature of the precepts?
Now, in paying homage to the fourfold assembly to save the multitude, what fault is there?
Therefore, both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna equally prohibit worldly etiquette; since they do not even accept such rites, the purpose of the ritual cannot be fulfilled.

Third, regarding the section on "Rejoicing" (anumodana) and below, which clarifies the meaning of rejoicing by way of persons and dharmas: one must possess three causes. "Peace and bliss" is the general [principle], while the "three causes" are the specific [factors]; thus it is said that "all are the single true reality" (ekalakṣaṇa), and again that "all possess the three causes."
"Reciting and chanting" below provides a detailed explanation of the three causes.
"Not slighting and deeply revering" below explains the phrase concerning the sublime benefits of circulation.
Within this, the first part directly applies the three and four [causes] to demonstrate circulation, while "in this way" and following conclude the argument.

Regarding the initial passage: if one attains the three dharmas that constitute the method for propagating the sutra, then both oneself and others will be saved. One should know that although these three dharmas follow the preceding chapter, they are in fact the three causes of this present chapter; therefore, they are also correlated with the four modes of peaceful conduct (*catur-āśvāsa-caryā*), the details of which may be understood by analogy with what precedes.

Regarding "not receiving the four or one," one should thoroughly internalize the aspect of not receiving the four or one even when faced with insults and the like; this is likewise the case in the fundamental stage.
The text merely provides a brief correspondence to the sūtra.

Regarding the passage beginning with “Not slighting those who are great and powerful,” followed by the phrase “and so forth,” this is for the purpose of proclaiming [the teaching] so that it may be heard.
One should explain that the "poison of strength" serves as the sign for hearing the Dharma in the future, just as described in the sutra concerning those who obtain benefit at a later time.
