Regarding the phrase "purity of mental action" followed by "and so forth," one should explain the correspondence between the three types of action and the three powers; furthermore, one should also correlate them with such things as robes, seats, and dwellings.
Supernormal powers are his chamber;
eloquence in exposition is his seat;
and sublime tranquility is his robe.
This may be understood by applying it broadly to all cases.

Regarding the phrase "those who revile" and so forth: even those who merely follow along [with such views] fall into suffering; thus, these constitute two drums—one for faith and one for revilement—serving as the two causes for future rebirth.
Question:
If one falls into suffering due to slander, why does a bodhisattva act as a cause for such suffering? Answer:

Even those who lack virtuous causes do not fall [into hell] merely by failing to slander; rather, it is because they slander that they fall into evil states, which must necessarily result from the benefit [of their actions]. It is like a person who falls to the ground and rises again from the ground; thus, through right slander, one is led from wrong falling.
Regarding the phrase "one should diligently practice the five kinds of conduct," these are the five kinds of conduct for Dharma masters.

Although the verse text mentions only the first fifteen and a half stanzas as describing the karmic rewards and the final four stanzas as exhortations to uphold [the teaching], according to this verse text, it should be understood that there is no description of the "double pointing"; rather, it describes only the two passages concerning the "double opening" and the "double exhortation."
In the initial section that opens the pair, the prose portion consists of two parts: the *vastu* (the event) and the *pūrvavastu* (the antecedent event).
Here, one and a half lines provide a general summary of the *vastu*, omitting details such as the eon and the country, followed by verses summarizing the *pūrvavastu*.

The prose section consists of three parts. First, one and a half verses introduce two individuals simultaneously; next, two and a half verses clarify gain and loss—of which the first one and a half verses concern gain and the subsequent half verse concerns loss; then, another half verse reiterates the theme of gain. Finally, from the words "Its sin" (*tasya pāpam*) downward, ten verses clarify the karmic retribution for praising and slandering, as well as correlating the past with the present.

Regarding the phrase "up to and including 'concentration' (*samādhi*)": this does not exclusively refer to heterodox outsiders; rather, any attachment to the Buddha’s provisional or ultimate teachings is termed "attachment" (*abhiniveśa*).
The analogy of the "ox-hide" and so forth is as explained in the fifth fascicle of the *Zhiguan* commentary.
To cling with a mind of attachment to the teaching of non-attachment is like tanning leather; it becomes even harder when exposed to the sun.

The loss of the True Dharma is like the decay of the body. Therefore, those who receive the provisional teachings cannot avoid slandering [the ultimate truth] while still at the stage of an ordinary person (bālapṛthagjana); thus, there are words of the perfect and real [teaching] that are neither accepted nor disparaged lightly.

Regarding the explanation of the title of the "Chapter on the Tathāgata’s Supernatural Powers": "Tathāgata" has been explained in the preceding "Chapter on Lifespan. As for "supernatural powers" (*ṛddhi*), "spiritual power" (*shen*) resides within; it is the essence and the fundamental principle.
"Power" (bala) refers to the function of efficacy; it is, in fact, activity itself.

The Buddha has already concluded his exposition on the power and function of the oral wheel regarding the provisional and ultimate aspects (honjaku) in the preceding section. Now, he again manifests this supreme function through the physical wheel, causing the teachings on the provisional and ultimate to circulate among the masses; therefore, it is said that "the essence is profound and the power is great."
The section beginning with "This word" specifically clarifies the purpose of the introduction;
the section beginning with "From this point on" provides the general purpose of the introduction.

Regarding the phrase "all" used for the assembly initially addressed, "all" refers to those from other directions, while "long-resident" refers to those originally transformed [by the Buddha]; thus, they should not be limited to the fourfold assembly or the eight classes of beings.
Therefore, the term "all" refers to the passage beginning from "and all others" onwards.
Regarding the "ten powers," the first five clearly elucidate the present circulation of the manifest and the trace, while the latter five collectively represent the inexhaustibility of the future.

Furthermore, among the first five [categories], the first causes the assembly to believe collectively in the unity of the fundamental and the manifested; the subsequent four are precisely the four "Ones" of the present.
The second [category] signifies that the principle of the two gates is one; because it is the object of wisdom, it is called the "object of wisdom."
The third manifestation clarifies the two gates of teaching, which is the unity of teaching.
The fourth manifestation enters the reality through the two gates, which is the unity of person.
The fifth manifestation destroys delusions through the two gates, which is the unity of practice.

Since the sixth section refers to three categories of people—the five thousand who were removed, those who were displaced, and those who lost their minds—these three examples are precisely those who attained benefit after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.

Regarding the term "capacity" (*ki*), its meaning should be understood comprehensively, as it encompasses the four "Ones" of the future; that is to say, it refers to obtaining the benefit of these four "Ones."
The four marks below distinguish the future [teachings] one by one; the text itself provides their names, yet each merely describes its essentials so as to form a single unity.

As for why these four are called "one" and not designated as "original" or "traced," it is because they pertain to the future; since they have not yet entered the reality [of the ultimate fruit], who would discuss their origin?
If one perceives the reality, one also perceives its source; therefore, it is summarized by saying, "The manifestation indicates what is to come.
"To come" (jiāng) means "that which is destined to be.
Within each of the first five sections, there are the three phases of the trace, the source, and the circulation.

In the initial passage, the title is first presented; from "Now this sutra" onwards, the preceding traces are described as being revealed; from "Internally secret" onwards, the preceding revelation of the traces to manifest the fundamental is described; from "Clarifying the three periods of time" onwards, the intermediate application is clarified; and from "Persons of merit" onwards, the primary intent of the supernatural power is shown.

Regarding the second passage, the first part indicates what is manifested by the divine power (*śakti*) of the present [Buddha], while the section from "the white curl above" (*ūrdhvakeśa*) downward describes how the divine power manifested in the *tracimukha* (trace-gate) is identical; because object and wisdom are united, one initially perceives the single principle.

"In the present 'Root Chapter'" (honmon) below, the preceding expressed meaning is restated: because one perceives the distant principle, the Path is increased and birth is diminished, reaching the vicinity of the ultimate.
Regarding "the emanated bodies" (fushin) and so forth, since these characteristics are identical, the benefit bestowed upon each respective land is likewise the same.

Regarding the third passage: first, it provides the title, clarifies the intent, and describes the characteristics; from "more than forty" onwards, it correctly describes the manifested traces; and from "desiring to" onwards, it clarifies the underlying meaning of these manifestations.
Regarding the phrase "possessing both," the matter refers to the original and the manifested [truths] being entrusted to others so as to extend through future ages.

As for the fourth section: the initial part designates the title and clarifies the intent; "rejoicing" below indicates the benefit of the manifested [truth]; "rejoicing in the perfect path" below indicates the benefit of the original [truth]; "rejoicing in all bodhisattvas" below indicates the benefit of its circulation; and "this one" below indicates the functional power of its circulation.

Regarding the fifth section, although it does not distinguish between the fundamental (hon) and the manifested (saku), one can understand that a single passage encompasses all five subsequent sections.

As for the essential conclusion consisting of four phrases: the two gates of the fundamental and the manifested each have their own principle (shū) and function (yō); yet, the substance (tai) of these two gates is no different in both places. This name [the title of the scripture] crowns these three and subsumes them all; how could the essentials of this entire work exceed this?
Therefore, these are summarized to facilitate circulation.
Regarding the "eight masteries," they are as explained in the *Commentary on the Śamatha-vipaśyanā*.
The phrase "the essential exposition in the sutra" and so forth describes the present intention.
Regarding the phrase "The Explanation of the Profound Matter of the Bodhimaṇḍa": "matter" refers to cause and effect; here, the bodhimaṇḍa is the fruit, and a fruit must necessarily have a cause.

Regarding the phrase "Explaining the Treasury by means of Bodhi": Bodhi is the wisdom that is capable of conforming to reality, and it must necessarily have an object of illumination; this object is the secret treasury (guhyakośa), for the subject reveals the object.
Regarding "explaining all dharmas by means of the turning of the wheel of Dharma": since there is a dharma that is turned, that dharma must necessarily have a name.

Regarding "explaining power and function by means of nirvāṇa": fulfilling the principle explains away doubts concerning the provisional; proclaiming extinction explains away doubts concerning the immediate. Although the primary tenet—whether immediate or remote—is the same in being designated as cause and effect, they are no longer separately judged.

Regarding the term "Āgama," it uses the small to testify to the great; whereas the former [the sūtras] concern themselves with phenomena (*dharma*), here we borrow them to testify to principle (*li*). Since opening the small leads directly to the great, they can serve as testimony.
As for the first verse of the stanzas, among the ten supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) mentioned therein, only five are present, as the latter five are missing.
The first five [categories] are directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*), so they are retained as essential; the latter two sets of five differ only in being present or future.
Since the future can be illustrated by the present, they are omitted.

Regarding the statement, "The final two lines of the entrustment (*parindanā*) provide a general verse on the four dharmas," it simply says "entrustment" up to "attaining the limit," which fully encompasses the four meanings; for all four meanings are themselves without limit (*ananta*).

Regarding the "Able to Maintain" section below, which consists of individual verses: within the first one and a half verses, the mention of "all phenomena" (sarvadharma) does not go beyond the transformer and the transformed, as well as the realizer and the realized.
Because there are no two vehicles and because it is not presented as a supplementary teaching, its Dharma is secret and subtle.
The two verses following "causing me" eulogize the supernormal power; since it speaks of "joy," this signifies that [the power] has been fully realized.
Next, one verse praises the secret essentials; its names are identical [to those previously mentioned] and thus easy to perceive.
The section beginning with "Regarding all dharmas" praises profound matters: it teaches that all bodhisattvas ultimately abide in the One Vehicle, and this vehicle consists of cause and fruit.
The final one and a half verses serve as a summary, which summarizes the four dharmas.
The phrase "If one can uphold" refers to upholding these four dharmas.
(From the *Fahua wenju ji*, Fascicle 10)
